query: Research on refractory multicomponent alloys has emphasized exceptional strength at room and elevated temperatures, while mechanical assessment has relied mainly on compression and has included relatively few tensile studies. WFeNiMo fragments released more chemical energy than tungsten-alloy fragments in thin-steel-target penetration tests, and HfZrTiTa0.53 was reported at 786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% terminal strain. This evidence establishes strength and energetic promise but leaves limited tensile ductility, load-bearing reliability, and processability unresolved. Subject to preserving strength and impact-triggered energy release, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention for HfZrTiTa0.53 that could improve tensile ductility and uniform elongation? Include the intervention, causal mechanism, directional or quantitative outcomes relative to the reported baseline, the applicable temperature, loading mode, and strain-rate limits, prior evidence from the cited studies, and matched compression, tension, and impact tests with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled warm rolling followed by an optimized annealing treatment will induce a bimodal (heterogeneous) grain size distribution in HfZrTiTa0.53, thereby improving its tensile ductility and uniform elongation without substantially compromising its high strength and impact-triggered energy release.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard HfZrTiTa0.53 produced via conventional processing with a homogeneous grain structure, showing a compressive yield strength of 786 MPa, compressive strength of 1314 MPa, and ~13.5% terminal strain.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to a post-processing thermo-mechanical procedure—a warm rolling process at a temperature below the recrystallization point followed by a precisely controlled annealing treatment—to develop a heterogeneous bimodal grain structure.
generation.conditions: Tensile tests performed at room temperature under moderate strain rates (on the order of 10^(-3) s^(-1)); compression and impact tests conducted under conditions matching the baseline evaluations.
generation.structural_mediator: A bimodal grain structure comprising fine grains that sustain high strength and coarser grains that promote strain partitioning and enhanced strain hardening (via back stresses), thereby delaying necking and increasing uniform elongation.
generation.mechanism: The induced heterogeneous microstructure facilitates progressive plasticity by enabling load transfer between fine and coarse regions. Coarse grains improve ductility through back stress hardening and dislocation accumulation at grain boundaries, while fine grains maintain the alloy’s high strength. This balance preserves the alloy’s impact-triggered chemical energy release capability.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in uniform tensile elongation from ~13.5% to approximately 18–20% with a yield strength maintained within ±10% of 786 MPa, while retaining similar impact energy release performance.
generation.baseline: HfZrTiTa0.53 processed conventionally exhibits limited tensile ductility (~13.5% elongation) despite its excellent compressive strength and impact energy release.
generation.boundary: This effect is predicted for room temperature tensile loading at moderate strain rates; the benefits and potential trade-offs under high strain rate or elevated temperature conditions remain uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal processing parameters (rolling reduction, warm rolling temperature, annealing time and temperature) required to achieve the desired bimodal microstructure without adverse effects on strength or energetic properties have yet to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfZrTiTa0.53 specimens: one set maintained under standard processing (control) and another set processed using the proposed warm rolling plus annealing treatment. Perform systematic room temperature tensile tests, along with matching compressive and impact tests on both specimen sets.
measurements: Grain size distribution and heterogeneity (via SEM/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the post-processed specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in uniform tensile elongation (i.e., fall short of reaching 18–20%) or if their yield strength and impact energy release decrease by more than 10% compared to the control samples, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

High-Temperature Mechanical Properties of NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 Refractory High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractThe NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 is a refractory multi-principal-element alloy with high strength and good ductility at room temperature. It is important for possible high-temperature applications to investigate the deformation mechanism of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy at different temperatures using tensile tests. In this investigation, the tensile tests were conducted at room temperature to 1273 K on sheet materials fabricated by cold rolling combined with annealing treatments. At 473 K, the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy exhibited a high tensile ductility (12%). At a testing temperature range of 673~873 K, the ductility was reduced, but the yield strength remained above 800 MPa, which is rare in most other alloys. The TEM investigations revealed that a dislocation slip controlled the plastic deformation, and the degree of deformation was closely related to the dislocation density. The true stress–strain curves of the alloy under different deformation conditions were obtained by tensile deformation at different deformation temperatures (673~873 K) and strain rates (0.001~0.0005 s−1). Achieving Excellent Strength-Ductility Balance in Single-Phase CoCrNiV Multi-Principal Element Alloy

Abstract: AbstractCoCrNi alloys exhibit excellent strength and ductility. In this work, the CoCrNiV multi-principal alloy with single-phase fine grained (FG) structure was prepared by rolling and heat treatment. The characteristics of deformation microstructures and mechanical properties were systematically investigated by scanning electron microscope (SEM) and transmission electron microscope (TEM). The results indicate that the CoCrNiV alloy successfully attains a yield strength of 1060 MPa while maintaining a uniform elongation of 24.1%. The enhanced strength originates from FG structure and severe lattice distortion induced by V addition. Meanwhile, the exceptional ductility arises from the stable strain-hardening ability facilitated by dislocations and stacking faults. The deformation mechanisms and the optimization strategies for attaining both strength and ductility are thoroughly discussed.Keywords: CoCrNiV alloy, multi-principal element alloy (MPEA), stacking fault, solid solution strengthening, fine grain (FG)

Negative enthalpy alloys and local chemical ordering: a concept and route leading to synergy of strength and ductility

Abstract: ABSTRACTSolid solutions are ubiquitous in metals and alloys. Local chemical ordering (LCO) is a fundamental sub-nano/nanoscale process that occurs in many solid solutions and can be used as a microstructure to optimize strength and ductility. However, the formation of LCO has not been fully elucidated, let alone how to provide efficient routes for designing LCO to achieve synergistic effects on both superb strength and ductility. Herein, we propose the formation and control of LCO in negative enthalpy alloys. With engineering negative enthalpy in solid solutions, genetic LCO components are formed in negative enthalpy refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs). In contrast to conventional ‘trial-and-error’ approaches, the control of LCO by using engineering negative enthalpy in RHEAs is instructive and results in superior strength (1160 MPa) and uniform ductility (24.5%) under tension at ambient temperature, which are among the best reported so far.
